units.sourceHTML: 3.8 Multiple commands syntax

units.text: There are several methods to specify multiple commands in a ⟦0⟧ program.
units.sourceHTML: There are several methods to specify multiple commands in a sed program.

units.text: Using newlines is most natural when running a sed script from a file (using the ⟦0⟧ option).
units.sourceHTML: Using newlines is most natural when running a sed script from a file (using the -f option).

units.text: On the command line, all ⟦0⟧ commands may be separated by newlines. Alternatively, you may specify each command as an argument to an ⟦1⟧ option:
units.sourceHTML: On the command line, all sed commands may be separated by newlines. Alternatively, you may specify each command as an argument to an -e option:

units.text: A semicolon (‘⟦0⟧’) may be used to separate most simple commands:
units.sourceHTML: A semicolon (‘;’) may be used to separate most simple commands:

units.text: The ⟦0⟧,⟦1⟧,⟦2⟧,⟦3⟧,⟦4⟧,⟦5⟧ commands can be separated with a semicolon (this is a non-portable GNU ⟦6⟧ extension).
units.sourceHTML: The {,},b,t,T,: commands can be separated with a semicolon (this is a non-portable GNU sed extension).

units.text: Labels used in ⟦0⟧,⟦1⟧,⟦2⟧,⟦3⟧ commands are read until a semicolon. Leading and trailing whitespace is ignored. In the examples below the label is ‘⟦4⟧’. The first example works with GNU ⟦5⟧. The second is a portable equivalent. For more information about branching and labels see ⟦6⟧Branching and Flow Control⟦7⟧.
units.sourceHTML: Labels used in b,t,T,: commands are read until a semicolon. Leading and trailing whitespace is ignored. In the examples below the label is ‘x’. The first example works with GNU sed. The second is a portable equivalent. For more information about branching and labels see Branching and Flow Control.

units.text: The ⟦0⟧,⟦1⟧,⟦2⟧,⟦3⟧ commands parse the filename until end of the line. If whitespace, comments or semicolons are found, they will be included in the filename, leading to unexpected results:

units.text: Any characters following the ⟦0⟧ command until the end of the line will be sent to the shell. If whitespace, comments or semicolons are found, they will be included in the shell command, leading to unexpected results:
units.sourceHTML: Any characters following the e command until the end of the line will be sent to the shell. If whitespace, comments or semicolons are found, they will be included in the shell command, leading to unexpected results:

units.text: In a substitution command, the ⟦0⟧ flag writes the substitution result to a file, and the ⟦1⟧ flag executes the substitution result as a shell command. As with the ⟦2⟧ commands, these must be terminated with a newline. If whitespace, comments or semicolons are found, they will be included in the shell command or filename, leading to unexpected results:
units.sourceHTML: In a substitution command, the w flag writes the substitution result to a file, and the e flag executes the substitution result as a shell command. As with the r/R/w/W/e commands, these must be terminated with a newline. If whitespace, comments or semicolons are found, they will be included in the shell command or filename, leading to unexpected results:
